column5: ancient paths, rest, and refusal to walk
column6: The commentary says the wretched person leaves the reminder beside his route; Jeremiah tells the people to seek the good ancient path and walk in it, but they answer that they will not walk there, joining guidance, a way, and its refusal.

column5: prepare a way in the wilderness
column6: The commentary develops a guide who goes ahead and a route made easy; Isaiah’s voice calls for the Lord’s way to be prepared in the wilderness, an explicit road-making image.

column5: mountains lowered and rough ground made level
column6: The commentary describes a long ridge that is nevertheless easier to climb; Isaiah pictures hills lowered and rough places leveled so a route can be traversed.

column5: donkey riders, saddle-related sitting, and walkers on the road
column6: The commentary brings together a riding cover, the mount, and a person’s route; Deborah’s song groups donkey-riders and walkers on the road with people sitting on a term sometimes understood as saddle-cloths, though that wording is uncertain.

column5: the Shunammite’s urgent ride on an ass
column6: The commentary describes a mount that follows readily and takes light steps; the Shunammite rides an ass and tells her servant not to slacken the pace, a concrete scene of directing a mount along a journey.

column5: God chooses a longer route because the people might turn back
column6: The commentary’s promise makes the way easier for its addressee; Exodus says God avoids the nearer Philistine route lest the people see war and return to Egypt, showing guidance adjusted to the travelers’ weakness.

column5: Adam sent from Eden to till the ground
column6: The commentary connects Adam’s expulsion from the garden with hardship; Genesis explicitly sends him out of Eden to work the ground, joining exile to the labor that follows.

column5: guide our feet into the way of peace
column6: The commentary develops guidance as showing a road and easing the traveler’s way; Zechariah’s prophecy says the dawn from on high will guide people’s feet into the way of peace, directly joining guidance, feet, and route.

column5: straight paths for the feet so the lame may be healed
column6: The commentary pairs a difficult ascent with weak, swaying walking; Hebrews commands straight paths for the feet so the lame limb will be healed rather than injured, joining path preparation to bodily weakness.

column5: strengthen weak hands and feeble knees
column6: The commentary’s secondary walking image is a weak person relying on support; Isaiah tells the hearers to strengthen weak hands and make firm feeble knees, a concrete bodily response to weakness.

column5: the lame leap like a deer
column6: The commentary links a mount’s light legs with a ridge that can be climbed; Isaiah says the lame will leap like a deer, turning impaired gait into agile movement.

column5: a lame man is raised by the hand and strengthened
column6: The commentary recalls a weak person who needs support to walk; Peter takes the man lame from birth by the hand and raises him, and his feet and ankles are strengthened, a concrete healing of unsupported gait.

column5: the healed man walks and leaps
column6: The commentary’s lexical image is a weak, swaying walker; after the healing in Acts, the man enters the temple walking, leaping, and praising God, showing the restored movement that support makes possible.

column5: make level paths for your feet
column6: The commentary’s mountain ridge is long but easier to climb and its route is made accessible; Proverbs urges the traveler to consider the path of his feet and make his ways firm, a practical image of preparing one’s course.

column5: human plans, the Lord directs the steps
column6: The commentary says the road can be the same while the traveler’s conduct differs; Proverbs contrasts a person’s plans with the Lord’s direction of his steps, clarifying the relation between human course and divine guidance.

column5: turn away from the evil path
column6: The commentary says the wretched person steps aside from the reminder; Proverbs commands the traveler to avoid the wicked path, turn from it, and pass on, a useful reversal in which one should leave the road rather than the warning.

column5: a man lame from birth is carried to the temple gate
column6: The commentary’s secondary walking image is a weak person who relies on support; Acts describes a man lame from birth being carried and placed at the temple gate, a specific scene of dependence before his healing.

column5: John identifies himself as Isaiah’s wilderness voice
column6: The commentary develops the guide and the way that is made ready; John applies Isaiah’s road-preparation oracle to his own role as herald, reading the route as preparation of people for the Lord’s coming.

column5: Balaam as one who leaves the straight way
column6: The commentary says a traveler can take a wrong course while the road remains; 2 Peter interprets Balaam as one who leaves the straight way for wrongdoing, giving the Numbers donkey episode an explicit moral reading of straying for gain.

column5: take the yoke, learn, and find rest
column6: The commentary’s easy mount follows its guide and carries its rider along the way; Jesus invites hearers to take his yoke and learn from him, promising rest for their souls, a distinct image of following under an easy discipline.

column5: the shepherd strengthens the sick and binds the injured
column6: The commentary’s guide imagery includes a weak walker who relies on support; God as shepherd says he will bind the injured, strengthen the sick, and seek the lost, joining direction with care for the weak.

column5: be swift as a deer and light as an eagle
column6: The commentary’s lexicon gives a mount that follows quickly and has light legs; Rabbi Judah ben Tema uses deer-swiftness and eagle-lightness as traits for doing the will of Heaven, turning animal agility into an ethical image.

column5: life and death are set before a person to choose
column6: The commentary links guidance with a traveler’s response and outcome; Sirach says life and death are before a person and the choice is given to him, extending the choice-of-way motif into Jewish wisdom teaching.
